item.title: - What gives birth to a person? What always runs about? What undergoes rebirth? What does a person fear? - Craving gives birth to a…
item.description:
- What gives birth to a person?
What always runs about?
What undergoes rebirth?
What does a person fear?
- Craving gives birth to a person,
The mind itself always runs about,
Beings undergo rebirth,
Suffering is what a person fears.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.55

item.title: “A person intoxicated by craving Throws himself into the stream Like a spider into its own web. But the wise cut it off, Having abandoned…
item.description:
“A person intoxicated by craving
Throws himself into the stream
Like a spider into its own web.
But the wise cut it off,
Having abandoned all suffering, they wander on without desire.”

From: Dhammapada 334-359

item.title: “Good sirs, what is suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, sickness is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, despair are suffering, not…
item.description:
“Good sirs, what is suffering? Birth is suffering, aging is suffering, sickness is suffering, death is suffering, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, despair are suffering, not getting what one wants is suffering; in short, the five clinging-aggregates are suffering. This, good sirs, is called suffering. Good sirs, what is the origin of suffering? It is craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, delighting here and there; that is, craving for sensual pleasures, craving for existence, craving for non-existence. This, good sirs, is called the origin of suffering.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 9 – Sammādiṭṭhisutta

item.title: “Monks, there are these three unwholesome thoughts: sensual thought, ill-will thought, harmful thought. And these three unwholesome thoughts are abandoned without remainder in one whose…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these three unwholesome thoughts: sensual thought, ill-will thought, harmful thought. And these three unwholesome thoughts are abandoned without remainder in one whose mind is well established in the four foundations of mindfulness or who develops the signless concentration. Monks, develop the signless concentration well. When the signless concentration is developed and cultivated, it brings great fruit and great benefit.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.80
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “And, monks, shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving, this body of the wise person is generated. That ignorance the wise person abandons. That craving…
item.description:
“And, monks, shrouded by ignorance and bound by craving, this body of the wise person is generated. That ignorance the wise person abandons. That craving the wise person destroys. Why is that? Monks, the wise person lives the holy life for the complete destruction of suffering. Therefore, with the breakup of the body, after death, the wise person does not go to another body. Not going to another body, he is freed from birth, aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair. I say that he is freed from suffering.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 12.19

item.title: “And how, monks, is there restraint? Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he is not attached to agreeable forms nor…
item.description:
“And how, monks, is there restraint? Here, monks, when a monk sees a form with the eye, he is not attached to agreeable forms nor repelled by disagreeable forms. He dwells with bodily mindfulness established, with an immeasurable mind. He knows as it actually is the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. Here, evil, unwholesome states that have arisen are abandoned without remainder. When he tastes a flavor … When he cognizes a phenomenon with the mind, he is not attached to agreeable phenomena nor repelled by disagreeable phenomena. He dwells with bodily mindfulness established, with an immeasurable mind. He knows as it actually is the liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom. Here, evil, unwholesome states that have arisen are abandoned without remainder. Thus, monks, is restraint.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.244

item.title: “And what, Ānanda, is the path, the way leading to the abandoning of the five lower fetters? Here, Ānanda, a monk, by the relinquishment of…
item.description:
“And what, Ānanda, is the path, the way leading to the abandoning of the five lower fetters? Here, Ānanda, a monk, by the relinquishment of attachments (upadhiviveka), by the abandoning of unwholesome states, by the complete calming of bodily coarseness, secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 64 – Mahāmāluṅkyasutta

item.title: “Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. And what, monks, is not yours? Form, monks, is…
item.description:
“Monks, whatever is not yours, abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. And what, monks, is not yours? Form, monks, is not yours — abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being. Feeling … Perception … Formations … Consciousness is not yours — abandon it. Abandoning it will lead to your happiness and well-being.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.33
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, if that monk, while attending to a different wholesome sign, still has evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, ill-will, and delusion arising, then that…
item.description:
“Monks, if that monk, while attending to a different wholesome sign, still has evil, unwholesome thoughts connected with desire, ill-will, and delusion arising, then that monk should examine the peril in those thoughts: ‘These thoughts are unwholesome, these thoughts are blameworthy, these thoughts lead to painful results.’ By examining the peril in those thoughts, those evil, unwholesome thoughts are abandoned and subside. With their abandonment, the mind becomes steadied, settled, unified, and concentrated.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 20 – Vitakkasaṇṭhānasutta

item.title: - “Friend, I do not abandon the present to chase after things subject to time. But, friend, I abandon things subject to time to chase…
item.description:
- “Friend, I do not abandon the present to chase after things subject to time. But, friend, I abandon things subject to time to chase after the present. The Blessed One has said that sensual pleasures are subject to time, of great suffering, of great despair — the peril in them is even greater. This Dhamma is visible here and now, not subject to time, inviting inspection, leading onward, to be directly experienced by the wise.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.20
